description: Next.js App Router supports server-side data fetching natively in Server Components using async/await. The extended fetch() API provides fine-grained caching control via cache and next.revalidate options. For non-fetch data sources (ORM, databases, SDKs), React.cache() provides per-request memoization and unstable_cache (or 'use cache' directive) provides persistent caching. The recommended pattern is to fetch data as close to where it is needed as possible, using Server Components for initial loads, leveraging request memoization to avoid duplicate fetches, and using parallel fetching to prevent sequential waterfalls. Client-side fetching (SWR, TanStack Query) is reserved for data that must be fresh after user interactions.

constraints.title: Explicit Fetch Cache Strategy Missing
constraints.problem: In the current Next.js model, fetch() requests are not cached by default. Developers who assume all fetch calls are cached (from older documentation) will serve uncached, fresh data on every request, eliminating the performance benefits of static prerendering.
constraints.whyItMatters: Without explicit caching, every incoming request triggers a fresh fetch to the upstream data source. At scale, this means O(requests * data_sources) upstream calls, increasing latency, cost, and the risk of rate-limiting by external APIs. Prerendering opportunities are lost when data is not cacheable.
forbiddenPatterns: Assuming fetch() is cached without explicitly setting cache: 'force-cache' or next.revalidate
Fetching the same data in multiple components without using React.cache() for deduplication
Omitting 'use cache' directive when data is suitable for caching across requests
Using unstable_cache without understanding its invalidation semantics
allowedPatterns: fetch(url, { cache: 'force-cache' }) for data that rarely changes
fetch(url, { next: { revalidate: 3600 } }) for time-based revalidation (ISR semantics)
fetch(url, { next: { tags: ['tag'] } }) combined with revalidateTag() for on-demand invalidation
'use cache' directive with cacheLife() for both data and UI component caching
unstable_cache() for ORM/database queries in the legacy model
React.cache() for per-request memoization of non-fetch data sources
productionRisks: Excessive upstream API calls leading to rate limiting
High database load from uncached queries
Increased latency for every page request
Higher infrastructure costs
Loss of static prerendering benefits
architectureImplications: Every data fetch in a Server Component should have an explicit caching decision
Shared data (fetched in multiple components) must use React.cache() or 'use cache' to deduplicate
Static content should be fully prerendered; dynamic content should be wrapped in Suspense
optimizationGuidance: Classify all data as: static (cache indefinitely), time-sensitive (ISR with revalidate), user-specific (no cache or short cache with tags), or real-time (no cache with Suspense streaming)
Use 'use cache' with cacheLife('hours') or cacheLife('days') for content that changes infrequently
quickFixes: Add { cache: 'force-cache' } to fetch calls for stable data
Add { next: { revalidate: 3600 } } for hourly revalidation
Add 'use cache' to data functions or components that should be cached
architectureSuggestions: Establish a team convention: every data-fetching function must document its cache strategy in a comment
Create a central data access layer where caching decisions are co-located with the data fetching logic

invalid: export async function getProducts() { return fetch('https://api.example.com/products').then(r => r.json()) } // Uncached, runs on every request
valid: export async function getProducts() { 'use cache'; cacheLife('hours'); cacheTag('products'); return fetch('https://api.example.com/products').then(r => r.json()) }

constraints.title: Fetch Data in Server Components — Avoid Client-Side Initial Data Loading
constraints.problem: Fetching initial page data in Client Components via useEffect or third-party libraries (SWR, TanStack Query) on mount creates a client-side waterfall: the HTML loads, JavaScript executes, then the data fetch begins, resulting in a blank or skeleton state that users must wait through.
constraints.whyItMatters: Server Components can fetch data before sending any HTML to the browser. By the time the user sees the page, data is already rendered. Client-side initial data fetching means users always see a loading state on first visit, degrading LCP and perceived performance. It also prevents static prerendering of the data.
forbiddenPatterns: useEffect(() => { fetch('/api/data').then(setData) }, []) for initial page data
SWR or TanStack Query for data that is available at render time and does not change via user interaction
Fetching data in Client Components when a parent Server Component could fetch it instead
Using getServerSideProps-style API Route fetching patterns in the App Router
allowedPatterns: async/await directly in Server Components for initial data
Passing fetched data as props from Server Components to Client Components
SWR/TanStack Query in Client Components for data that must refresh on user interaction
The use() hook in Client Components to consume a promise passed from a Server Component (streaming pattern)
productionRisks: Degraded LCP from client-side data loading waterfalls
Flash of loading state on every page visit
Loss of prerendering and CDN caching for data
Unnecessary client JavaScript for data fetching libraries
architectureImplications: The App Router's server-first design eliminates the need for client-side initial data fetching in most cases
Client-side data fetching libraries should be used for mutations, polling, and user-interaction-driven refreshes, not initial loads
optimizationGuidance: Migrate useEffect data fetching to Server Components progressively, starting with the most critical above-the-fold content
Keep SWR/TanStack Query for truly dynamic, user-interaction-driven data needs
quickFixes: Move the fetch() call to the parent Server Component and pass data as props
Make the page component async and await the data directly
architectureSuggestions: Establish a rule: initial data is always fetched server-side. Client-side fetching is for subsequent mutations and real-time updates only.

valid:
// page.tsx (Server Component)
export default async function ProductPage({ params }) { const product = await getProduct(params.id); return <ProductDetail product={product} /> }

constraints.title: Use React.cache() to Deduplicate Non-fetch Data Requests
constraints.problem: When multiple Server Components in the same render tree need the same data (e.g., user session, product details), each component calling the data source independently results in duplicate database queries or API calls within a single request.
constraints.whyItMatters: React automatically memoizes fetch() requests with the same URL and options within a render pass. But for ORM queries, database clients, and custom async functions, no deduplication occurs by default. Without React.cache(), the same database query may execute dozens of times per request in a complex component tree.
forbiddenPatterns: Calling the same database query function in multiple components without React.cache() wrapping
Fetching the same user session in every component that needs it
Prop-drilling data from a top-level component to avoid duplicate fetches (obscures data dependencies)
allowedPatterns: import { cache } from 'react'; export const getUser = cache(async (id) => db.user.findUnique({ where: { id } }))
Using React.cache() for all data access functions in the Data Access Layer
Combining React.cache() with 'server-only' for safe, reusable, memoized server data utilities
productionRisks: N×M database queries per request where N is the number of components and M is the number of shared data sources
Database connection pool exhaustion under load
Increased latency from redundant upstream calls
architectureImplications: React.cache() scope is per-render pass (per-request), unlike persistent caches
A Data Access Layer using React.cache() enables safe co-location of data fetching in each component without performance overhead
optimizationGuidance: Wrap all data access functions in the DAL with React.cache()
This allows any component to call getUser(id) knowing it will only hit the database once per request regardless of how many components call it
quickFixes: import { cache } from 'react'; then wrap the data function: export const getData = cache(async (id) => { ... })
architectureSuggestions: Build a Data Access Layer (lib/dal.ts) where every exported function is wrapped with React.cache() and import 'server-only', creating a safe, deduplicating, server-only data interface

invalid:
// Called by 5 components — 5 DB queries per request
export async function getUser(id) { return db.user.findUnique({ where: { id } }) }

constraints.title: Do Not Call Route Handlers from Server Components
constraints.problem: Server Components calling internal Route Handlers (fetch('/api/...')) to load data creates an unnecessary HTTP roundtrip through the network stack on the same server.
constraints.whyItMatters: A Server Component calling its own Route Handler sends an HTTP request from the server back to itself (or to another server instance in distributed deployments). This adds network latency, bypasses the database connection pool optimization, and prevents prerendering. The correct approach is to call the data access function directly.
forbiddenPatterns: fetch('/api/products') inside a Server Component when a direct DB call is available
Using Route Handlers as an abstraction layer between Server Components and data sources
allowedPatterns: Calling data access functions or ORM methods directly in Server Components
Using Route Handlers only for external API consumers or Client Component fetches
fetch() to external third-party APIs from Server Components
productionRisks: Unnecessary HTTP roundtrip latency (10-100ms overhead per call)
Loss of prerendering capability
Increased server load from loopback requests
Connection pool waste
architectureImplications: Route Handlers are for external API consumers, not for Server Component data access
Server Components have direct server-side access — use it
optimizationGuidance: Create a Data Access Layer that can be called directly by Server Components
Route Handlers delegate to the same DAL functions, not the other way around
quickFixes: Replace fetch('/api/data') with direct import and call of the data access function
architectureSuggestions: Structure: Server Component → calls DAL function → queries DB. Not: Server Component → fetch('/api') → Route Handler → calls DAL → queries DB.

invalid: export default async function Page() { const res = await fetch('/api/users'); const users = await res.json(); return <UserList users={users} /> } // Unnecessary HTTP hop
valid:
import { getUsers } from '@/lib/dal'
export default async function Page() { const users = await getUsers(); return <UserList users={users} /> }

constraints.title: Use 'use cache' or unstable_cache for Non-fetch Data Sources
constraints.problem: Database queries, ORM calls, and custom async functions do not benefit from Next.js's extended fetch() caching. Without explicit caching via 'use cache' (Cache Components model) or unstable_cache (legacy model), these operations run on every request.
constraints.whyItMatters: fetch() is automatically extended by Next.js to participate in the Data Cache. ORM queries (Prisma, Drizzle, TypeORM) and database clients (pg, mysql2) are plain JavaScript calls with no inherent caching. They must be explicitly wrapped to gain persistent caching across requests.
forbiddenPatterns: ORM queries in Server Components without 'use cache' or unstable_cache when the data is suitable for caching
Database queries running on every request for data that changes infrequently
Omitting cacheTag() on cached functions that need on-demand invalidation
allowedPatterns: Cache Components model: async function getProducts() { 'use cache'; cacheLife('hours'); cacheTag('products'); return db.select().from(products) }
Legacy model: unstable_cache(async () => db.select().from(products), ['products'], { tags: ['products'], revalidate: 3600 })
Combining React.cache() for per-request memoization with unstable_cache for persistent caching
productionRisks: Database overload from uncached queries under production traffic
High latency from per-request database calls for static content
Missed ISR opportunities for content that changes infrequently
architectureImplications: ORM queries require explicit caching annotations — they are not auto-cached like fetch()
The 'use cache' directive extends caching to any async operation, not just fetch()
optimizationGuidance: Classify all ORM/database queries by update frequency and apply appropriate cacheLife profiles
Add cacheTag() to all cached queries to enable surgical on-demand invalidation after mutations
quickFixes: Add 'use cache' and cacheLife() to ORM query functions in the DAL
Wrap with unstable_cache() for the legacy model
architectureSuggestions: Co-locate caching decisions with data access functions in the DAL: each function declares its cache strategy and tags

invalid: export async function getProducts() { return db.select().from(products) } // Runs on every request
valid: export async function getProducts() { 'use cache'; cacheLife('hours'); cacheTag('products'); return db.select().from(products) }

constraints.title: Implement the Preload Pattern for Parallel Data Fetching with Dependencies
constraints.problem: When one piece of data depends on another (sequential dependency), but other independent data can be fetched in parallel, failing to initiate parallel fetches early causes the overall response to be slower than necessary.
constraints.whyItMatters: JavaScript's async model allows initiating multiple promises before awaiting any of them. The preload pattern kicks off data fetching before any blocking await, allowing parallel execution even when some sequential logic exists. Missing this optimization causes request waterfalls where sequential awaits compound latency.
forbiddenPatterns: Awaiting sequential fetches when later fetches could start earlier
Not starting data fetches until after conditional logic completes when the condition does not affect the data
allowedPatterns: Calling preload(id) before any await to kick off background data loading
Promise.all() for fully independent parallel fetches
Starting fetches for likely-needed data before confirming they are needed (with proper error handling)
productionRisks: Unnecessary request latency from sequential data loading that could be parallel
P99 latency degradation on pages with multiple data dependencies
architectureImplications: The preload pattern works because React.cache() memoizes the result — the preloaded data is reused when the component awaits it later
optimizationGuidance: Always check: can I start any fetch earlier? If yes, use Promise.all() or the preload pattern.
quickFixes: Replace: const a = await fetchA(); const b = await fetchB() With: const [a, b] = await Promise.all([fetchA(), fetchB()])
architectureSuggestions: Establish a convention: data dependencies at the top of Server Components are always declared before any await, using Promise.all() for independent fetches

invalid:
const isAvailable = await checkAvailability(id)
const item = await getItem(id) // Waits for checkAvailability to finish first — unnecessary
